bibliography.abstract: Turbo roundabouts minimize weaving conflicts by introducing raised lane separators within the circulating lanes compared with conventional multilane roundabouts. Although widely used in Europe, turbo roundabouts are relatively new in the US. The California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) installed a rotor turbo roundabout in San Benito County in 2024. This research analyzed driver behavior and evaluated safety performance at this newly built turbo roundabout by performing descriptive analysis and statistical modeling. Approximately 5% of vehicles made prohibited lane changes within circular lanes, particularly during left-turn movements. The factors affecting the prohibited lane-change model indicate that lower vehicle speeds on circular lanes, light vehicle types, and vehicle headways are significantly associated with the likelihood of lane-changing events. The speed choice model indicated that lower approach speeds, heavy vehicle types, left-turn movements, and smaller circular lane radii reduced vehicle speeds on circular lanes. An early traffic analysis applying the extreme value theory (EVT) captured the relationship between conflict estimates and observed crashes. Based on average post encroachment time (PET), extreme conflicts were caused primarily by improper lane changes and failure to yield. The turbo roundabout substantially lowered crash severity and eliminated speeding-related crashes. A total of 76% of postinstallation crashes were attributed to unfamiliarity and right-of-way violations, and 22% were due to navigational errors. These findings underscore the need for improved dissemination of proper turbo roundabout driving information and appropriate signage to facilitate safe lane selection and prevent prohibited lane changes within circulating lanes. The findings of this study contribute to a broader understanding of turbo roundabout performance in the US and can be used to refine design and safety analyses based on driver behavior in the US.

en.caveats: The findings are based on a single newly installed turbo roundabout in California, meaning the observed driver confusion and crash patterns may reflect initial novelty effects rather than long-term steady-state behavior.
en.what: This study analyzed driver behavior and safety outcomes at the newly constructed rotor turbo roundabout in San Benito County, California, using descriptive analysis, statistical modeling, and extreme value theory. The analysis revealed that 5% of drivers made prohibited lane changes within the circular lanes, particularly during left turns, with lower speeds, light vehicle types, and specific vehicle headways increasing the likelihood of these violations. While the turbo roundabout eliminated speeding-related crashes and reduced overall crash severity, 76% of post-installation crashes were linked to driver unfamiliarity and right-of-way violations, and 22% were caused by navigational errors.
en.why: It provides some of the first empirical evidence on how US drivers adapt to the physical lane separators of turbo roundabouts, identifying specific behavioral failure points like improper lane changes and yielding failures that can be addressed through targeted signage and design adjustments.
